PEP26 SeaRam

Navarrete

Background
The Promoting Electric Propulsion (PEP) competition challenges students in designing
and building a small craft boat to race in one of six divisions. These divisions include: crewed
planing, crewed displacement, uncrewed autonomy, uncrewed over-the-horizon, uncrewed open,
and uncrewed budget warrior. Since 2018, universities across the United States have participated
in this event with the sponsorship of The Office of Naval Research (ONR). ONR works to “plan,
foster, and encourage scientific research in recognition of its paramount importance as related to
the maintenance of future naval power, and the preservation of national security.” The ONR
developed the PEP competition for the Navy in order to attract engineering students to electric
propulsion. This allows them to collect research data that students conduct with naval technology
that is modular and scalable [1].
The American Society of Naval Engineers (ASNE) is a non-profit organization that
advances the knowledge and practice of naval engineering, supports the development of ships
and ship systems, promotes collaboration between industry and academia, and fosters
professional development of naval engineers. They are governed by a Council of Directors which
includes the president, three vice presidents, and a chief executive officer [1]. The ONR and
ASNE work together to inspire upcoming engineers to get into the field of electric propulsion.
The three goals for VCU’s PEP26 team are to: improve battery performance and battery
mounting, optimize angle of attack and add an in-line pump filter, and add autonomy. The team
is participating in the autonomy division this year. VCU has participated in the PEP competition
for the past three years. The 2024 team designed an RC boat that had significant issues in weight
distribution and power management. These areas were redesigned and improved by the 2025
team. The 2025 team replaced the one main motor design with a dual motor setup. These new
motors are a 6-pole brushless type (SSS 56123-V2 KV500). Eight LiPo batteries (10k mAh
22.2V 25C) were configured in parallel to maximize available capacity. A set of two 3D printed
battery trays were designed for the batteries. The batteries and ballast payload were held in place
with an internal wooden support structure. Two small pumps provided system cooling for the
two electronic speed controllers (ESC) and two motors. The 2024 and 2025 teams participated in
the uncrewed open division. The 2025 team placed 12 th out of 30th in their race.

Design & Analysis
Drivetrain
The driving force of the SeaRam is provided by two 6-pole brushless motors (SSS 56123V2 KV500) as shown in Figure 1. The combination of a higher pole count and a 500 KV rating
provide increased torque compared to 2 and 4 pole motors. This choice is critical to improve
acceleration while the boat is carrying a payload between 30-60 lbs. The dual motor setup was
selected by VCU’s PEP25 to maximize torque and thrust. The motor mounts originally sourced
from Bonzi Sports were replaced with custom 3D printed mounts. The new mounts fit the
shorter, new 18” driveshafts which replaced the 24” driveshafts from last year. The new
driveshafts are displayed in Figure 2. The dual motors are fitted with water-cooling jackets to
prevent damage caused by overheating. This decision was validated through a thrust calculation
from The Propeller Handbook [2]. Assumptions applied in the calculation included: a target
speed of 30 mph, a drivetrain and propeller efficiency of 0.5 (worst-case), a hull wake drag
coefficient of 0.95, and a motor power output of 3 kW.

Figure 2. Drive shafts

Figure 1. Dual Motors

Electrical System
The previous 2025 team boat’s electrical system prioritized Ah capacity for operational
time in their power system setup. It utilized eight 6S batteries connected in parallel, represented
as a 6S8P setup, which provided 22.2V with 80 Ah of capacity. Their 6S8P design maximized
amp-hour capacity but provided a relatively low voltage output of 22.2V. As a result, the speed
output of the boat was significantly less when compared to a higher 44.4V voltage setup. The
boat’s actual operational time on race day was reduced due to rough water which increased
power consumption to maintain forward momentum.

pages.text:
VCU

PEP26 SeaRam

Navarrete

The 2025 team boat’s electrical system has been redesigned to provide increased torque
and thrust. The eight 6S batteries are connected in four parallel packs of two batteries in series
represented as a 12S4P setup. This new setup provides a 44.4V output with 40 Ah of capacity.
The current used by the dual motors is reduced due to the higher voltage input. Two waterproof
150A circuit breakers (Figure 3) were installed into the positive main voltage side of the system
to provide electrical safety. The 150A breakers are setup to trip before permanent damage can
occur to the motors with the lowest max amperage rating of 188A. The higher ratings of the
batteries at 250A, and the ESC at 300A are also protected. A fuse was installed in series with the
pump system to provide electrical safety. The pump runs on a smaller standalone battery.
One 6S battery in the system has a 10 Ah capacity rated at 25C that outputs 22.2V. The
12S4P setup provides a measured maximum voltage of 50.4V at full charge which is below the
competition’s 55V limit. Mounted busbars provide an electrical path for the eight batteries. The
system also includes an emergency shutoff switch (Figure 4) that disconnects main voltage to
the dual ESCs and dual motors.

Figure 4. Emergency shutoff switch
Figure 3. 150A breaker

Propulsion System
The propulsion system utilizes two 500 KV motors with neodymium magnets that deliver
up to 3 kW each. The new HobbyWing 300A HV V4 ESC provides efficient motor control and
Bluetooth telemetry. The telemetry provides recorded testing data that includes the ESC’s
voltage, temperature, and current. The motor’s RPMs are also estimated. A Spektrum DX6C
transmitter and a SR515 receiver are used for remote user control. The transmitter and receiver
were kept the same from last year’s team.
System cooling for the motors and ESCs is provided by a new 1.2 gpm SeaFlo 12V
pump. The water intakes built into the rudders supply the pump with water. A smaller,
standalone battery supplies power to the pump. The new ESCs and pump provide the dual
motors with increased reliability, improved power management, accessible data collection, and
enhanced cooling.

Wiring Setup
The wiring from the bus bars to the breakers and ESCs is 6 AWG using appropriately
sized ring terminals and EC8 connectors. XT90 connectors and ring terminals are used with the
battery packs to the bus bar. XT90 connectors can handle 90A continuous current while EC8 can
handle 180A continuous current. The boat’s wiring diagram is displayed in Figure 5 below.

Figure 5. Wiring Diagram

Hull
The hull design utilized in this project remains the same as the previous year’s team. As a
result, previous calculations performed by the 2025 team can be reapplied. The hydrodynamic
and vector flow analysis calculations were reviewed and modified to provide visualization and
performance predictions under expected operating conditions. A simplified model of the hull,
both with and without strakes, was analyzed to evaluate their impact on stability and handling.
Environmental water conditions representative of the intended operating site was incorporated
into the simulations. Initial hydrodynamic diffraction analysis was performed, followed by
response analysis where wave frequency and water velocity were adjusted to replicate real-world
motion. These simulations provided insight into how the hull behaves at peak operating
conditions, particularly when accounting for payload and internal system weight. Results showed
that the hull without strakes exhibited noticeable lateral drift and, over extended simulation time,
a tendency to become unstable and tip. In contrast, the hull design including strakes
demonstrated significantly improved stability, with only minor drift that can be corrected
through trim adjustments. This confirms the importance of strakes in maintaining directional
control and overall performance. To further evaluate performance, a multiphase flow vector
analysis was conducted using the straked hull configuration at the expected maximum operating
speed as shown in Figure 6, Figure 7, and Figure 8. The simulation indicated that the wake

cavitation under real operation conditions which can reduce efficiency and cause long-term blade
erosion. In contrast, the 2.7-inch propeller displayed more uniform pressure distribution across
both the face and back of the blades. The reduction in concentrated low-pressure pockets
suggests a lower cavitation risk at the target RPM.
The CFD simulations confirm that the 2.7-inch diameter, 4.32-inch pitch propeller
provides superior thrust and torque output while exhibiting more stable pressure distribution and
reduced cavitation risk as shown in Figure 13 and Figure 14. Although it requires slightly more
time to reach steady-state operation which is seen during testing, its performance advantages
make it the more suitable configuration for optimal propulsion under peak operational
conditions. These calculations were experimentally confirmed by the PEP26 team. Relevant
online information [3] about a boat’s pitch was also examined. As a result, the 2.7 in. propeller
with a 4.32 in. pitch remains the current choice for the SeaRam.

While the boat is moving forward, the flow rate increases due to the rudder mounted
water intakes. The effective heat transfer rate increases due to the increased water velocity. A
single 3S 11.1V battery using a step-up converter powers the pump at 12V. The SeaFlo Pump is
rated for 1.2 gpm. After testing, the measured flow rate was 6.579 gpm at standstill. This flow
rate is well above the required flow rate needed for the two motors and ESCs. The pump was
selected to provide the highest amount of cooling possible from the available water intakes. This
redesign would ensure effective cooling during max throttle operation.
Limited US and world parts availability resulted in metric and imperial conversions being
required in the design. About half the parts already integrated in the design utilized the metric
system. These included the motors, ESCs, rudder intakes, barbed y fittings, and outlets. The
other half which used the imperial system included the pump, pump filter, hose clamps, reducers,
and tubing. The barbed y fittings allow one larger pump to cool components. Extensive testing
was conducted to ensure leak free and reliable connections.

Autonomy
The SeaRam’s autonomy is dependent on the Cube Orange flight controller which
provides onboard processing and integrated sensors for autonomous navigation. The Cube
Orange follows US regulations regulating radio frequency safety [4]. The system’s full
capabilities are shown in Figure 16. The PEP26 team will be utilizing only a few of the sensors
available. The controller enables real-time GPS positioning which allows the boat to
continuously track its location, speed, and heading during operation. The Cube Orange interfaces
with a GPS module and onboard telemetry system to transmit live position data to a ground
control station. The Cube Orange can follow pre-programmed waypoints or navigation
commands sent from the control station. It can also perform path corrections based on sensor
feedback. During varying environmental conditions expected at Portsmouth City Park, it is
expected to maintain its stability. The Cube mounting fixture is displayed in Figure 17. The
Cube Orange is also compatible with the ArduPilot ecosystem. This feature enables mission
planning, system monitoring, and post-run data analysis, which are essential for validating
autonomous performance and improving system reliability for competition.

Payload and Battery Restraints
The V-hull shape proved to be a challenge for both the 2025 and 2026 team. The payload
and battery restraint system would need to be designed carefully due to the unusual angles
imposed by the hull. The PEP26 team decided to use a similar system as last year to hold the 30
lb. required payload. This included reusing a locking rail system sourced from McMaster-Carr
that supported the payload and battery trays. The locking platforms are guided by aluminum rails
connected to 2x4 wooden planks that are attached to the hull. One set of rails on each side carry
four batteries which are held by 3D printed battery containers (Figure 18). The containers are
bolted onto a plank of wood that provides structural support. This new design was selected over
an earlier design that mimics the payload system due to the rails diverging further apart towards
the boat’s bow. As such, the rails did not retain their intended parallel design. The new design
retains the easy installation and removal of the batteries in previous designs. The payload
required adding 3D printed extensions to the rails which allowed for a wooden beam between the
two rails. The 3D printed payload container was drilled into wood for stability as shown in

Payload and Battery Restraints
        The V-hull shape proved to be a challenge for both the 2025 and 2026 team. The payload
and battery restraint system would need to be designed carefully due to the unusual angles
imposed by the hull. The PEP26 team decided to use a similar system as last year to hold the 30
lb. required payload. This included reusing a locking rail system sourced from McMaster-Carr
that supported the payload and battery trays. The locking platforms are guided by aluminum rails
connected to 2x4 wooden planks that are attached to the hull. One set of rails on each side carry
four batteries which are held by 3D printed battery containers (Figure 18). The containers are
bolted onto a plank of wood that provides structural support. This new design was selected over
an earlier design that mimics the payload system due to the rails diverging further apart towards

Testing and Risks
Steering System
The SeaRam is equipped with dual rudders that allow for bi-directional turning as shown
in Figure 20. During testing, the rudders had an issue of a pin coming loose. This caused the
rudder to only be held by the cooling tubes. Our team replaced the missing pin with a bolt to
improve rudder stability. A risk assessment was conducted of other potential issues and listed in
Table 1.

Figure 20. Rudder System

Table 1. Risk Matrix

Testing was performed at maximum turning radius and full speed to test the limits of the
SeaRam. Stress-testing capabilities before the race is crucial to spot weaknesses and avoid more
potential failures. The addition of differential thrust will assist the rudders in steering. This
should lower the forces exerted on the linkage and reduce the risk of rudder stall, servo failure,
and/or rudder structural failure.

Cooling System
A series of tests will be conducted to verify the boat’s seaworthiness, endurance, and
overall performance. Testing will take place at Wilde Lake with the help of Brian, a local
community resident. This lake provides sufficient space for the SeaRam to go full throttle for
extended periods of time. Testing was conducted over a period of weeks which included testing
for water leaks, power usage, maneuverability, acceleration, and angle of attack. The team's first
priority was to keep the boat’s interior dry. Multiple tests were performed on the water pump’s
hose clamps, inlets and outlets, and rudder arms. Table 2 below displays the on-bench testing
before the filter was installed.
Table 2. Flow Rate Test Results (without filter)

The previous PEP2025 team had a sand infiltration issue that caused premature pump
failure. The new PEP2026 SeaRam design incorporated an in-line filter with a 40-micron rating
to specifically filter sand and small particulates. Concerns about the filter’s effect on the heat
transfer rate were examined and tested in Table 3. The heat transfer rate was minimally reduced
by about 500-600W, or 10%.
Table 3. Flow Rate Test Results (with filter)

The throttle percentage (blue) and ESC temperature (green) are plotted over time in
Figure 21 below. The highest recorded ESC temperature at max throttle remains below 30°C.
This is well within the listed safe operating range for the ESC with a maximum operating
temperature of 120°C. Motor temperatures cannot be directly recorded at this time unless a
thermal sensor is attached to its casing.

Drivetrain
The two ESCs shown in Figure 22 record data during testing. The data is accessed using
the proprietary Hobbywing HW Link V2 app. This app provides live metrics of the motor’s
performance and power consumption. Parameters such as RPM, throttle percentage, ESC
voltage, current, and temperature are graphed. Figure 23 displays the current draw when the
throttle is set to 100%. The measured power draw was recorded at 3,276W at 46.8V and 70A.
Figure 24 displays the current draw when the throttle is around 50% throttle in short intervals
(500ms). Current draw was recorded low because of the very short bursts of throttle. The
recorded voltage (purple) is properly below the 55V limit set by the PEP competition. Figure 24
displays the worst-case performance in a run that pulled around 100A. This was caused by the
driveshaft mechanically starting to bind in the stuffing tube. As a result, the throttle decreased
while the current draw increased. Previously, the PEP25 team used an S-shaped stuffing tube
with sharp bends that caused a lot of friction and binding of the driveshaft. Surface temperatures
of the stuffing tube measured with a thermocouple recorded a temperature of 110°F after 30
seconds of full throttle under no load. This serious design flaw forced the team to perform an
immediate overhaul of the driveshaft and stuffing tube system. No sharp bends were placed onto
the new stuffing tube and alignment was prioritized. The friction and binding issues were greatly
reduced which restored power output stability to the propellers.

Payload Balancing
Several water tests were performed to balance the weight of the batteries and payload
across the guide rails inside the boat. The boat moves nearly level with a centralized payload and
battery positioning in Figure 25. Conversely in Figure 26, moving the payload towards the stern
increases the lift of the bow. This increased the angle of attack of the boat which created a
rooster tail towards the back. The previous PEP25 team angled the propellers at 5° from the
waterline. During testing, this angle was retained for acceleration, deceleration, and turning.

Conclusion
The development of the SeaRam represents a continuation, and refinement, of previous
Virginia Commonwealth University PEP team work, with a focus on improving power, tuning,
and autonomous capability while maintaining compliance with ASNE competition rules.
Through the careful improvement of propulsion, electrical, structural, and control systems, the
team has optimized the vessel to meet the competition’s demanding performance requirements.
The propulsion system, consisting of dual 500 KV brushless motors paired with an optimized
propeller geometry, provides the necessary thrust to achieve target speed while maintaining
stable operation with the addition of a payload. Supporting systems such as the redesigned
electrical system, upgraded cooling system, and refined drivetrain reduce inefficiencies and
thermal loading that enable sustained high-power operation. Computational simulations,
including CFD propeller analysis and hydrodynamic hull evaluation, further validated design
decisions and demonstrated improvements in stability, thrust generation, and cavitation
reduction.
In addition to propulsion and structural improvements, the integration of autonomous
control through the Cube Orange flight controller introduces reliable navigation and datacollection. This system allows the SeaRam to execute waypoint navigation while providing realtime telemetry and post-mission performance analysis. Combined with a modular payload and
battery mounting system designed to accommodate the V-hull geometry, the vessel maintains
structural stability while supporting the required payload capacity. Testing conducted under real
operating conditions verified cooling performance, power consumption, and maneuverability,
while also identifying areas for mechanical refinement such as drivetrain alignment. Overall, the
SeaRam demonstrates a balanced design that integrates mechanical, electrical, and autonomous
subsystems into a cohesive platform capable of meeting the operational goals of the ASNE
competition while providing a strong foundation for future team development and iteration.
